interest: This file provides historians with valuable contemporaneous insight into Japan's pre-World War II transition toward a state-managed war economy and its aggressive policy of industrial autarky. It highlights the strategic cooperation between Japanese government ministries, zaibatsu and industrial conglomerates (such as Nissan, Mitsui, and Mitsubishi), and the military—particularly the Kwantung Army—to systematically squeeze out dominant American corporations like Ford, General Motors, and Chrysler in favor of domestic manufacturing. Furthermore, the diplomatic exchanges and cross-references regarding Central China and Manchuria vividly illustrate how Japan used puppet regimes (such as Manchukuo and the Renovation Government) and pseudo-private monopolies to circumvent international treaties and dismantle the Open Door policy well before the outbreak of the Pacific War.
overview: This file (State Department decimal 894.602, covering March 1934 to January 1939) documents the Japanese government's progressive implementation of state industrial control, monopolistic cartels, and subsidies, as well as their direct impact on Western commercial interests and the Open Door policy in Japan, Manchuria, and occupied China. Centered largely on communications from U.S. Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo, the records detail Japan's concerted campaign to foster an autarkic domestic motor-car industry by imposing discriminatory licensing regulations, raising tariffs, and blocking American automotive giants like Ford, General Motors, and Chrysler from expanding or assembling locally in Japan and Manchukuo. The file also chronicles diplomatic tensions surrounding Japanese industrial encroachments in occupied China following the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War, notably British and American protests against the formation of the Japanese-backed Central China Silk Yarn Company monopoly over sericulture and cocoon supplies, as well as the infringement of the Belgian Tramway and Electric Company's franchise in Tientsin.

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an instruction sent to the American Embassy in Tokyo to report on the efficiency of the Japanese business machine resulting from trade subsidies.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 30 sent on March 14, 1934, at 7 p.m., to the American Embassy in Tokyo, originally filed under 611.9417/17. The telegram instructs diplomatic officers in Japan to investigate and report on the efficiency of the Japanese commercial system bolstered by direct and indirect governmental subsidies and grants-in-aid aimed at export promotion. It serves to cross-index export subsidy intelligence into the industrial monopolies decimal classification 894.602.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 30 on Export Trade Subsidies

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1067 concerning proposed control of the motor-car industry in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 1067 of November 28, 1934, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo to the Secretary of State, filed under 894.797/4. It records the subject as proposed governmental control of the motor vehicle industry and commerce in Japan and Manchukuo. The cross-reference ties broader Japanese industrial regulation files to specific automotive trade policies.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 1067 on Motor-Car Industry Control

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on emerging Japanese policies and military actions designed to establish state control over the automobile industry and marginalize American manufacturers in Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that following the model of the petroleum monopoly laws, Japanese government ministries and the military are devising a comprehensive control system over the automotive sector in Japan and Manchukuo. The program entails licensing vehicle assembly, subsidizing domestic manufacturers, raising import tariffs on chassis and finished vehicles, and developing a standardized 'New Economic Car' for mandatory official use. In Manchuria, the Japanese-dominated Towa Jidosha Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha was established at Mukden to assemble vehicles under tariff protection, with plans for an eventual sales monopoly. Grew documents how the Japanese military actively obstructed American companies, blocking General Motors from selling equity to Nippon Sangyo, preventing Ford from purchasing manufacturing land, and forcing the Kwantung Leased Territory government to cancel Chrysler's assembly permit in Dairen.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1067 from Grew on Proposed Control of the Motor-Car Industry (Pages 1-6)

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 165 regarding Cabinet approval of a draft bill to control the Japanese automobile industry.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 165 sent at noon on August 10, 1935, by Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo, originally filed under 894.797/6. It summarizes the Japanese Cabinet's approval of a draft bill for the control of the automobile industry intended for the upcoming Diet session. Key provisions mentioned include licensing requirements favoring majority Japanese-owned firms.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 165 on Automobile Control Bill

subfiles.about: A telegram transmitting the core provisions of a Japanese Cabinet-approved draft bill imposing licensing and ownership restrictions on the automotive sector.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville informs the Secretary of State that the Japanese Cabinet approved a draft bill on August 9, 1935, to regulate the motor vehicle industry. The bill mandates licenses for motor-car assembly and parts manufacturing, restricting new licenses strictly to corporations organized under Japanese law with majority domestic shareholding. Existing foreign assembly operations are restricted to their current output capacity, with any future facility or production expansion placed under strict government control.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 105 from Neville on Automobile Industry Control Bill

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram authorizing the presentation of a diplomatic note to Japan regarding the Open Door in China.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 339 sent at 2 p.m. on October 1, 1938, classified under 693.002/352a. The telegram quoted the text of a diplomatic note that the Department of State authorized the American Embassy in Tokyo to deliver to the Japanese Foreign Office at its discretion. The subject of the communication concerns the defense of the Open Door principle against Japanese encroachments in China.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 339 on the Open Door in China

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits a British diplomatic note protesting Japanese monopolization of the silk industry in Central China.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwards to Washington a copy of a formal communication delivered by the British Embassy to the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 3, 1938. The note details the detrimental impact on foreign interests caused by the creation of the Central China Silk Yarn Company. Grew notes that this entity functions in practice as a Japanese-controlled monopoly covering silk reeling and cocoon markets in Wusih, Soochow, and Hangchow.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3331 from Grew on British Note Regarding Central China Silk Monopoly

subfiles.about: A British diplomatic note expressing grave concern over the creation of a Japanese silk monopoly in Central China that threatens British filatures.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy draws the attention of the Japanese Foreign Ministry to reports that major Japanese concerns—including Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Katakura, Kanegafuchi, and Gunze—have formed the Central China Silk Yarn Company with an 8-million-yen capital. The note points out that the enterprise aims to establish an exclusive monopoly over raw silk purchasing, filature operations, and cocoon crops in Wusih, Soochow, and Hangchow. It emphasizes that this monopoly would severely harm British commercial operations in Shanghai, notably Jardine, Matheson and Company, and requests official assurances that no such monopolistic disruption will occur.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Note No. 159 Protesting Central China Silk Monopoly
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits the Japanese Foreign Office's official note verbale denying that the Central China Silk Yarn Company constitutes a monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwards a translated copy of Japanese Note Verbale No. 161, dated October 21, 1938, received via the British Embassy. The communication responds to British inquiries concerning the newly established Central China Silk Yarn Company. In the note, the Japanese Foreign Office maintains that the company is not an exclusive monopoly and is not intended to prejudice the vested commercial rights of third-power nationals.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3444 from Grew Transmitting Japanese Reply on Silk Monopoly

subfiles.about: The Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs denies allegations of a silk monopoly, characterizing the Central China Silk Yarn Company as a developmental enterprise.
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Foreign Ministry replies to the British Embassy's note of October 3, 1938, regarding the Central China Silk Yarn Company. The Ministry explains that the company was authorized in mid-August 1938 by the Renovation Government of China as a joint Sino-Japanese legal corporation headquartered in Shanghai with a capital of 8 million yen. While admitting that the firm operates silk reeling facilities and handles cocoon processing and silkworm egg distribution to foster sericulture, the note insists that it does not monopolize these activities or obstruct foreign vested interests.
subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Ministry Note Verbale No. 161 on Central China Silk Yarn Company

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 3597 regarding Japanese infringement upon the franchise of the Belgian Tramway and Electric Company in Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Despatch No. 3597 sent on January 12, 1939, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, originally filed under 893.78/143. It records reports of a Japanese firm infringing upon the established monopoly rights of the Belgian Tramway and Electric Company in Tientsin. It notes that a British Embassy protest addressed to the Japanese Foreign Ministry on January 9, 1939, was enclosed with the despatch.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 3597 on Belgian Tramway Rights in Tientsin

subfiles.about: Concluding section of Despatch No. 1067 analyzing Japanese military restrictions on American automakers in Manchuria and the closing of the Open Door.
subfiles.summary: In these concluding pages of Despatch No. 1067 (scanned out of order at the end of the file bundle), Ambassador Grew discusses how the Kwantung Army forced the cancellation of Chrysler's assembly plant permit in Dairen to prevent private competition with Towa Jidosha Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha in Mukden. While acknowledging that some American representatives believed Japanese manufacturers could not match American quality or price given limited domestic market size, Grew cautions that Japan's intense nationalism and organizational capabilities should not be underestimated. He concludes with a stark warning that if these automotive control schemes succeed, the Open Door in Manchuria will be further closed to American commerce.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1067 from Grew on Proposed Control of the Motor-Car Industry (Pages 7-8)
